summary: TerraMatch is a remote-sensing pipeline and interactive dashboard that identifies Earth analog sites for Moon and Mars missions. It measures two independent properties of a landscape from open NASA data. The first is surface ruggedness, expressed as an Angular Vector Ruggedness Measure (VRM) and Rugged Hazard Area (RHA) computed with OpenCV. The second is radiative behavior, expressed as Broadband Shortwave Albedo (BSA) derived from Landsat 8–9, Mars Global Surveyor TES, and LROC WAC data. Any Lunar or Martian coordinate is compared against two curated databases of 50 Earth analog sites each (50 Mars analogs and 50 Moon analogs) and ranked on three leaderboards: roughness/roamability-based match, thermal and solar match, and a combined planetary twin (the best analog site overall with the most identical metric values to the inputed lunar/martian site). This addresses the challenge by replacing subjective, appearance-based analog selection with a repeatable, quantitative comparison that works on Earth, the Moon, and Mars. It matters because multi-billion-dollar rover, lander, and spacesuit programs cannot afford blind spots—testing on a poorly matched Earth site masks critical mechanical and safety failures until hardware is already on the Moon or Mars.
details:
TerraMatch matches Lunar and Martian coordinates against two curated databases of 50 Earth analog sites (spanning volcanic fields, impact craters, hyper-arid basins, and polar deserts) using orbital imagery alone. Built in Python with FastAPI, OpenCV, NumPy, and GDAL, the platform runs two parallel engines and a weighted Euclidean matching layer on standard consumer hardware without needing scarce elevation models.

The ruggedness engine extracts surface roughness directly from optical brightness variations using basic photoclinometry principles. Raw orbital images are resized to a standard 800-pixel width and masked to exclude deep shadows (pixel intensity 5 or lower) and glare (250 or higher) so unobserved ground is never scored as flat terrain. Valid pixels are smoothed with a 5-by-5 Gaussian blur and mapped to a fixed zero-to-one reflectance scale without per-image contrast stretching. Treating image brightness as topographic relief, a Scharr edge-gradient filter computes horizontal and vertical intensity derivatives, scales them across a 15-by-15 pixel neighbourhood window, and projects each pixel into a three-dimensional unit surface-normal vector perpendicular to the local slope. By averaging these unit vectors over the 15-by-15 window, uniform slopes produce aligned vectors with a resultant length near one, while rugged terrain causes directional scattering and vector cancellation. Taking the inverse cosine of the resultant vector length yields the angular dispersion in radians without wrap-around errors, which is divided by a fixed 90-degree ceiling to yield a bounded zero-to-one Vector Ruggedness Measure (VRM). Pixels exceeding a VRM threshold of 0.25 are tallied as the Rugged Hazard Area (RHA) fraction and blended at 50 percent opacity with a terrain roughness difference highlighting map-like overlay using colour shades to indicate between smooth (blue shades) and sharp/jagged (red, yellow, green, other brighter shades) for maneuverability indication - which can also reveal micro-craters, ridges, and lava flows.

Instead of downloading massive planetary map files, the albedo engine uses SpatioTemporal Asset Catalog (STAC) APIs to fetch exact 30-kilometre regional tiles resampled onto a 128-by-128 grid in real time. To standardise surface reflectivity across all three bodies onto a unified zero-to-one Broadband Shortwave Albedo (BSA) index, Earth Landsat 8 and 9 surface reflectance bands (blue, red, near-infrared, and two shortwave infrared bands) are equalised using Liang’s (Liang 2000) narrowband-to-broadband weighted linear regression equation. For Mars, pre-calibrated global albedo mosaics are streamed directly from the Mars Global Surveyor Thermal Emission Spectrometer (MGS TES), while Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter Camera Wide Angle Camera (LROC WAC) photometric mosaics are streamed for the Moon and scaled by a 0.75 broadband conversion factor.

Queried targets are compared against the Earth databases using span-normalized squared Euclidean distances across three specialised leaderboards: Maneuverability and Roughness Match (equally weighting VRM and RHA), Reflectivity and Thermal Match (measuring absolute BSA difference), and Dual-Best Planetary Twin (weighting BSA at 50 percent, VRM at 25 percent, and RHA at 25 percent). While this enables rapid hardware test-site screening from open orbital imagery, current limitations include VRM acting as a dimensionless roughness proxy rather than a true physical slope angle, alongside differing native sensor resolutions across Earth (30 meters), the Moon (100 meters), and Mars (7.4 kilometers). Future iterations will integrate high-resolution stereo elevation models like HiRISE and LROC NAC where available, add seasonal solar incidence-angle modeling for polar illumination extremes, and support direct JSON exports for rover traverse planning.
